approvedEntries.name: Mulberry
approvedEntries.scientific: Morus rubra — red mulberry, the native tree of the eastern US. Also Morus alba (white mulberry, naturalized from China across all 48 states and now the commonest mulberry in the country), Morus microphylla (Texas mulberry, of southwestern limestone canyons) and, escaped from cultivation on the Pacific coast and in the Southwest, Morus nigra (black mulberry). All are edible. Note that M. rubra x M. alba hybrids are now so widespread that most "red mulberries" in settled eastern country are hybrids — this matters for conservation, not for safety.
approvedEntries.habitat: Two very different trees under one name, plus a third in the Southwest. Red mulberry is a tree of rich, moist, well-drained alluvial ground — floodplain and bottomland hardwood forest, stream terraces, cove bottoms, the lower third of slopes — on deep fertile loam, often over limestone in the interior. It grows with sugar maple, basswood, white ash and beech in the north, and with sweetgum, hackberry, box elder, sycamore, green ash, black walnut and pawpaw in bottomlands. Critically for a forager: it is shade-tolerant enough to sit in the understory for decades, and a red mulberry under closed canopy sets almost no fruit. The trees worth walking to are the ones with light on the crown — in a gap, a blowdown, a field edge, a fencerow. White mulberry wants disturbed ground and full sun: fencerows, alley margins, railroad embankments, vacant lots, hedgerows, ditch banks, the shelterbelts it was planted into by the million across the Plains, and in the arid West the irrigation ditches and cottonwood-willow riparian strips it has invaded. Texas mulberry is a different creature again — a shrub or small tree of dry limestone and igneous canyon slopes, arroyos and dry streambeds through the Edwards Plateau, Trans-Pecos, southern New Mexico and Arizona, with fruit a third the size and generally ripening in May. Wherever mulberry grows it grows inside the bird-sown hedgerow guild: pokeweed, black nightshade, bittersweet nightshade, poison ivy, hackberry, black cherry and elderberry are all planted by the same birds into the same seam of ground. Habitat can therefore NEVER be used to rule out pokeweed or the nightshades. They are not merely nearby — they are the plants standing under, and growing up through, the tree you are about to shake.
approvedEntries.indicator: Look down, not up. From late spring into midsummer a mulberry announces itself as purple-black splatter — crushed fruit and bird droppings staining sidewalk, driveway, car roof, fence rail and the ground for ten or fifteen feet around — long before you pick the tree out of a hedgerow. Mulberries follow perch lines, because birds plant them there: fencerows, the drip line of hedgerows, the ground beneath power and telephone lines, the edges of old barn lots and homesteads. Wildly different leaf shapes on the same twig clinch it — unlobed, one-lobed "mitten", and deeply three- or five-lobed, all within a foot of each other. Almost nothing else in North America does that so freely, and every one of those leaves bleeds white latex from a broken stalk within seconds.
approvedEntries.parts: Fully ripe fruit only — the compound fruit (syncarp), which comes off the twig as one unit rather than as loose berries. No cooking, soaking or leaching is required or useful: ripe mulberry is safe raw, and it is one of the very few wild fruits with no preparation step at all. Everything hazardous about this tree is a ripeness question. On a dark-fruited tree, ripe means uniformly deep purple-black right to the tip with no red or pink drupelets left, slightly dull rather than glossy, soft enough to squash between two fingers, and detaching at the lightest touch — if you have to pull, it is not ready. Colour is USELESS on white mulberry, which is the mulberry most Americans actually stand under: ripe M. alba fruit may be white, cream, lavender, pink or near-black depending on the individual tree, so judge entirely by feel — translucent, soft, honey-sweet, dropping on its own. Unripe fruit, and the milky latex that runs from every green part (leaf stalks, twigs, green fruit), cause nausea, vomiting, cramping and diarrhoea; NC State's toolbox additionally records CNS stimulation and hallucination from unripe fruit and raw shoots. Cooking does not fix unripe fruit — there is no boil-and-leach protocol here, only waiting, so do not put green fruit in a pie on the theory that heat sorts it out. The latex is a contact irritant that raises welts on people who handle a lot of green material, and Morus pollen is a heavy, medically significant aeroallergen — El Paso, Tucson and Las Vegas all banned planting it for that reason. Mulberry leaves are made into tea and eaten cooked in parts of Asia, but they carry both the latex and the iminosugar 1-deoxynojirimycin, which measurably lowers blood glucose; anyone on diabetes medication should leave the leaves alone. Ripe fruit raw, or in pies, cordial, jam and syrup — it is very low in acid, so nearly every preserving recipe wants added lemon.

lookalikes.name: Pokeweed / pokeberry (Phytolacca americana)
lookalikes.tell: THE ONE THAT MATTERS, and it is a bucket-contamination risk as much as an identification one. Pokeweed is a herb, not a tree: one fleshy, hairless stem — showy magenta to purple-red, up to 2 in thick and 10 ft tall — that dies to the ground every winter, so there is no bark and no woody twig anywhere on it. Snap it: it is juicy and green inside and bleeds no white latex. Every mulberry twig, leaf stalk and green fruit bleeds white latex within seconds of a break. That tell works all season and on every part. Fruit architecture decides the rest. A pokeberry is ONE round berry, flattened top and bottom like a miniature pumpkin with about ten visible ribs, up to about 3/4 in wide, sitting on its own short stalk with a small green star of sepals on top, one of dozens along a drooping raceme; the berries come off individually. A mulberry is a single compound fruit — roughly fifty fused drupelets in an elongated bumpy cylinder 1/2 to 1 1/2 in long — with no calyx, no internal stalks, and it detaches as one piece. Squash one: a pokeberry holds about ten hard, flat, lens-shaped black seeds in a ring, and mulberry seeds are soft and unnoticeable. Both stain the same magenta, so juice colour proves nothing. Season, honestly: across most of the range pokeberries do not blacken until late July, after mulberry has largely finished, so for a northern picker the overlap is only the last weeks — but NC State records pokeweed fruit displaying June through November, and along the Gulf and through the mid-South ripe pokeberries are hanging while mulberries are still dropping. Do not treat the published "pokeweed is a fall berry" line as protection. Place gives no protection either: pokeweed is a bird-sown plant of fencerows, alley margins, hedgerows and tree bases — the exact ground white mulberry occupies — and it commonly grows straight up through the low branches of a hedgerow mulberry to head height, so its racemes hang among the mulberry's own fruit. This is why the tarp method needs a sorting step: shaking a tree onto a sheet takes everything over the sheet. All parts are toxic (root worst): saponins phytolaccatoxin and phytolaccigenin plus a mitogenic lectin, causing severe vomiting, cramping, bloody diarrhoea, hypotension and, in bad cases, seizures. The National Capital Poison Center states that although rare, death may occur, and children are the usual patients — a 20-year Kentucky poison-centre series found a median patient age of 3 with pokeberries implicated in 93.9% of exposures. Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) rather than waiting to see.

lookalikes.name: Bittersweet nightshade / climbing nightshade (Solanum dulcamara)
lookalikes.tell: A slender woody vine that climbs into hedgerow shrubs and low tree branches — very often into the very mulberry you are picking — so its fruit dangles among mulberry leaves at exactly picking height, which no amount of tree identification protects you from. Berries are single smooth egg-shaped ovoids about 1/2 in long on individual stalks with a green calyx, in loose drooping clusters, ripening green to yellow to orange to glossy scarlet from July onward across the northern half of the country; the flowers, if any are left, are unmistakable purple stars with a protruding yellow beak. Nothing about it is a bumpy compound cylinder, the stems carry no milky latex, and bruised foliage smells foul. The specific trap: red is a stage a real mulberry passes through, so the reasoning "it's red, it must be an unripe mulberry" is precisely the reasoning that gets a handful of nightshade into the bucket. Check that the fruit is bumpy and compound and attached to a woody twig bearing alternate, evenly toothed, sometimes lobed leaves. Solanine-type glycosides; a leading cause of paediatric plant-poisoning calls, with vomiting, diarrhoea, drowsiness and, in quantity, weakness and slowed breathing.

lookalikes.name: Black nightshade — eastern, American and European (Solanum ptychanthum, S. americanum, S. nigrum)
lookalikes.tell: The other black-berried plant standing under an urban mulberry all summer. A knee- to waist-high branching herb with no latex, no bark and no woody twigs; white five-pointed star flowers with a yellow cone of anthers; and small round glossy black berries about 1/4 to 3/8 in across in loose drooping umbel-like clusters of three to ten, each a single sphere on its own stalk with a small green calyx. Fruits June through October — squarely inside mulberry season in every region, unlike pokeweed — and thrives in the disturbed ground, garden edges and vacant lots where white mulberry lives. A mulberry is an elongated compound cylinder on a woody twig; these are separate round spheres on a green herb. Green unripe berries are the dangerous stage (solanine-type glycosides, with documented child fatalities), and even fully ripe berries of this group are eaten in some cuisines only after cooking. Do not export mulberry's "ripe means safe" rule onto them.

lookalikes.name: Paper mulberry (Broussonetia papyrifera)
lookalikes.tell: Same family, same copious milky latex, same absurdly variable lobed and mitten-shaped leaves, and one of the most abundant weed trees in southeastern and mid-Atlantic cities — where it is simply called "mulberry" by everyone who lives under it. Separate it by touch and by fruit shape, both of which work through the whole harvest season. Leaves: NC State describes paper mulberry as rough on top and hairy beneath, and the new stems as hairy brownish-red; run a thumb under the leaf and you get grey-green velvet. A true mulberry leaf is green and hairless or nearly so beneath except along the veins, and its twigs are essentially smooth. Arrangement helps too — all Morus leaves are strictly alternate, while paper mulberry's are alternate but often opposite or whorled, especially near shoot tips. The fruit settles it outright: paper mulberry makes a round BALL about 3/4 to 1 1/4 in across, orange-red to purple-red, with fleshy hair-like drupelets sticking out all over it like a sea urchin, on a long stalk. A mulberry is an elongated dark cylinder with drupelets packed smooth and flat. One more clue: paper mulberry is dioecious and most naturalized colonies are male root-suckers that never fruit at all, so a "mulberry" that has never set fruit in a season of watching is worth a leaf-underside check. Eating the fruit will not poison you — it is insipid and hairy rather than dangerous — but the latex raises a rash on many people and the male pollen is a documented severe aeroallergen.

lookalikes.name: Osage orange / hedge apple (Maclura pomifera)
lookalikes.tell: Not a fruit confusion — a tree confusion, and a common one, because this is the other milky-latex Moraceae tree and it was planted into Midwest and Plains hedgerows interwoven with mulberry, so the two stand in the same fencerow with identical bleeding twigs. Anyone keying out "hedgerow tree with white sap" as Morus needs to rule this out first. Osage orange carries stout straight thorns 1/2 to 1 in long in the leaf axils (Morus is thornless — this alone decides it, in leaf or bare), unlobed glossy leaves that taper to a long point with entire margins rather than the toothed and variously lobed leaves of mulberry, and deeply furrowed orange-brown bark. Its fruit is unmistakable once present: a wrinkled green softball 3 to 5 in across, on the ground in October. There is no stage at which it can be picked as a mulberry, but there is every chance of standing under one in June deciding you have found a mulberry that failed to fruit. Inedible rather than poisonous; the latex is a contact irritant.

lookalikes.name: Poison ivy and eastern poison oak (Toxicodendron radicans, T. pubescens)
lookalikes.tell: Belongs here because of what you touch, not what you pick: the hairy poison-ivy vine climbs the trunks of hedgerow and vacant-lot mulberries, and the standard mulberry harvest has you put both arms around that trunk and shake it. Before you touch a trunk, look for the fuzzy rope — poison ivy's aerial rootlets make the bark look shaggy and hairy where the vine runs up it. On the leaves: poison ivy is trifoliate, three fully separate leaflets each on its own short stalk with the middle one distinctly longer-stalked than the two side ones, glossy, with a few irregular teeth or none. A deeply three-lobed mulberry leaf reads as trifoliate to a beginner but is one blade — the lobes are joined to each other and share a single leaf stalk, the margin is evenly toothed all the way round including into the sinuses, and the surface is sandpapery. The decider is sap: break a mulberry leaf stalk and it bleeds white latex within seconds; poison ivy bleeds clear sap that oxidises black in minutes. Urushiol dermatitis, and burning brush or vines produces smoke that can put people in hospital.

approvedEntries.harvest: Take as much as you can carry — this is one of the few wild foods where over-harvest genuinely is not a concern. A mature mulberry sets far more fruit than any person can gather, drops most of it uneaten, fruits over two to four weeks rather than all at once, and picking fruit does not harm the tree at all. White mulberry in particular is a listed invasive: restricted in Wisconsin, prohibited in Indiana, restricted in Ohio, and profiled as invasive by extension services across the Midwest and East. The real conservation problem runs the other way — M. alba hybridises freely with native red mulberry and is genetically swamping it, which is why M. rubra is rare or tracked at the northern edge of its range (rare but native in Minnesota, Endangered in Canada). So: eat all the white mulberry you like, and do not help it move. Do not transplant seedlings, and do not scatter seed. METHOD, with the step the folk version leaves out: spread a sheet or tarp, shake the branches, and only truly ripe fruit lets go — far faster than picking and self-selecting for ripeness. Then SORT WHAT LANDS before it goes anywhere near a pot. The tarp catches everything over the tarp, which includes leaves, twigs, green fruit, insects, and any pokeweed raceme or nightshade stem growing up through the low branches. Never pour a tarp straight into a bucket and a bucket straight into a pan. TIMING across the range: south Florida and the lower Rio Grande from late March; the Gulf, central Texas and the lower South late April into May; the mid-South and mid-Atlantic late May into June; the Midwest and Northeast June into July (Minnesota Extension puts white mulberry ripe around the 4th of July); the interior West and Pacific Northwest July into early August. Texas mulberry in the southwestern canyons is mostly a May fruit. Any one tree carries ripe and unripe fruit simultaneously for weeks, so return every two or three days rather than stripping it once. WHERE NOT TO PICK: skip trees on busy road verges, in old orchard or industrial ground, and in municipal rights-of-way that may be sprayed — mulberry has no skin to speak of and cannot be scrubbed. Wash in cold water; a 15-minute soak in about 5% brine (1 tbsp salt to 2 cups water) followed by a cold rinse floats out spotted-wing drosophila larvae, which are near-universal in ripe mulberry by the back half of the season. That soak is a quality step, not a safety one. Get permission for private land, and check local rules before harvesting street trees.

notes.name: Blackberry & black raspberry
reasons: No missing deadly lookalike. Every berry that actually lands in a blackberry bucket is covered: pokeweed, moonseed and belladonna as deadly; black/bittersweet nightshade, Virginia creeper, buckthorn and baneberry as toxic. I hunted specifically for bramble-entry gaps (privet, Lantana, Aralia spinosa, Daphne laureola, Cocculus carolinus) and none is a deadly omission — each is a single smooth drupe on an unarmed plant that the entry's own drupelet test settles, or is seasonally offset.

The core ID rule is sound and beginner-proof: an aggregate of many drupelets on a white receptacle, on a woody armed cane. No North American toxic fruit is an aggregate of drupelets, and every deadly lookalike listed is a single smooth berry on an unarmed herb or vine — so the primary tell does not fail on the part or season harvested (ripe fruit, Apr–Oct).

Tells are fruit-in-hand and season-correct, and the entry actively kills three unreliable published tells rather than repeating them: the red-stem pokeweed rule (correctly noted that stems are green through early summer), the matte-vs-shiny ripeness rule (correctly limited to cultivated types and R. allegheniensis/armeniacus), and the grape 'no forked tendrils' rule for moonseed. It also anticipates the specific trap it creates by saying red Rubus fruit is merely astringent, by naming baneberry and bittersweet nightshade as the plants that rule kills people with.

The other 16 sources return 200. The belladonna facts themselves are standard and correct, so this is a citation defect, not a safety one.

reasons: SCHEMA: passes exactly. Parsed /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/data/foraging-species.ts (23 entries) — all use the identical 12-key set (caution, habitat, harvest, indicator, lookalikes, months, name, parts, regions, scientific, sources, terrain) and this entry matches it with no extra or missing keys. caution 'expert' is legal; all ten lookalikes use legal danger values (3 deadly, 7 toxic — no illegal 'harmless'); terrain woodland/edge/wetland/upland/disturbed all exist in the Terrain union; regions northeast/midwest/southeast/southcentral are all valid RegionIds per src/data/seasonal-regional.ts.
CAUTION LEVEL: 'expert' is required and correct — belladonna, moonseed and sheep laurel are all deadly-rated, so the rule (deadly lookalike exists => expert) is satisfied, not a judgement call.

MONTHS: [4,5,6,7,8] is 0-indexed May–September, correct for a union across the four listed regions (southeastern V. myrsinites/V. darrowii from late spring, northeastern lowbush late July into September). It is internally consistent with the entry's own text, which places moonseed (Aug–Sep) and pokeweed (Aug–Oct) 'inside the late blueberry window' — the season is not truncated in a way that would drop a lookalike out of scope.

REGIONS: correctly scoped. mountain and west are excluded, and the western blue Vaccinium (V. membranaceum, V. deliciosum, V. ovalifolium, V. scoparium) are explicitly declared out of scope in prose rather than being crammed into regions[]. Same region set as the existing Sassafras entry, which covers comparable eastern acid-upland ground. Ozarks/Ouachitas/east Texas mentioned in habitat are all covered (MO=midwest, AR=southeast, OK/TX=southcentral).

CORPUS CONSISTENCY: verified every shared lookalike against its grading elsewhere in the file — belladonna 'deadly' (burdock entry, line 169), moonseed 'deadly' (elderberry, line 670), pokeweed 'toxic' (lines 194/680/1079), buckthorn 'toxic', privet 'toxic', Virginia creeper 'toxic' (elderberry entry, line 695, with the same explicit reasoning about the disputed historical fatal reports), Toxicodendron 'toxic' (sassafras, hickory, elderberry entries). Sheep laurel 'deadly' matches the sassafras entry's grayanotoxin-heath lookalike at line 1474, which names Kalmia angustifolia, Lyonia and Leucothoe and rates them deadly. Nothing here contradicts the Aesculus-deadly-everywhere precedent.

NO MISSING DEADLY LOOKALIKE FOUND: I tested the entry's own decision rule (woody twiggy shrub + small simple alternate leaves + five dry teeth at the blossom end + cloud of tiny soft seeds) against the eastern blue/black-fruited flora. Everything that passes it is harmless and is named as such (black huckleberry, serviceberry, chokeberry, dangleberry, farkleberry). Everything deadly in range is caught: belladonna and the black nightshades by calyx position and herbaceous habit, moonseed by the single crescent seed and twining habit, the grayanotoxin heaths by leaf texture plus the fact that they bear capsules and not fruit.

THE STANDARD-TEST TRAP IS HANDLED: the entry does the single most important thing for this species — it names the 'five-pointed star' rule as the test belladonna passes, and forces the reader to check WHICH END the star is on. That is the actual failure mode in reported poisonings and most guides get it wrong.

TELLS ARE IN-SEASON AND STRUCTURAL: no tell depends on a feature absent at picking time. The entry explicitly retires the flower-based tells that are useless in fruit — blueberry's urn-shaped bells, Clintonia's yellow lily flower, Virginia creeper's scarlet autumn foliage — and it flags that 'look for a thorn' clears the wrong buckthorn, since glossy buckthorn is the thornless one that invades highbush ground.

THE REAL HAZARD IS CORRECTLY IDENTIFIED AND CONTROLLED: the likeliest route to harm here is not a berry mix-up but grayanotoxin leaf arriving as debris from the mat. The entry states that grayanotoxins are heat-stable and non-volatile (so cooking does not fix it), forbids raking and fist-stripping, and applies a mechanical control twice — hand-pick berry by berry, then tray-sort every leaf, twig and capsule. Crucially it does not let that bleed into the parasite question, where heat DOES work; the two are kept separate and both are stated correctly.

PREPARATION IS SPECIFIC WHERE IT MATTERS: Echinococcus multilocularis guidance carries actual numbers (>=70 C / 158 F held 5 minutes; eggs infective 240 days at -18 C so home freezing does not work; ~-83 C for 48 h needed) and the numbers match the cited Veit 1995 and Federer 2004 papers. The withdrawal of the old 'cook the ankle-height fruit, eat the waist-height fruit raw' rule is a strengthening, not a relaxation — it replaces a false control with an explicit decision.

NON-BLOCKING — sheep laurel leaf arrangement: Kalmia angustifolia leaves are opposite OR in whorls of three; the tell states only 'set in WHORLS OF THREE'. A picker holding an opposite-leaved sprig could wrongly clear it. Suggest 'opposite or in whorls of three'. The alternate-vs-not contrast with blueberry holds either way, and the tray-sort control is species-agnostic, so this is not a safety failure.

NON-BLOCKING — consider adding bog rosemary (Andromeda polifolia / A. glaucophylla): it is a grayanotoxin heath standing in the same sphagnum rim the entry sends you to for highbush, and unlike sheep laurel its leaves are ALTERNATE, narrow and whitish beneath — which defeats the entry's own laurel leaf rule. Distinguishing marks are strongly revolute margins, chalky-white underside, evergreen leathery texture and dry capsules rather than fruit. The 'remove every leaf' instruction already covers the actual exposure route, which is why this is a suggestion rather than a block.

NON-BLOCKING — Lyonia is bundled into the sheep laurel tell, but Lyonia leaves are alternate and thin-ish, so only the 'dry hard capsules, never a blue berry' half of that tell applies to it. Worth one clause saying so.

NON-BLOCKING — the scientific field claims the western blue Vaccinium 'are a separate entry'; no huckleberry entry exists in the corpus yet. Either add one or soften the wording to 'not covered here'.

NON-BLOCKING — the endemic-range raw-fruit position ('accept a small risk knowingly') would be better with one carve-out: children and immunocompromised readers should get cooked fruit only, since alveolar echinococcosis runs worse under immunosuppression.

BEGINNER TEST: a beginner following this entry as written picks by hand into a shallow tray, sorts every leaf and twig out before cooking, checks which end the crown is on, checks shrub-vs-herb-vs-vine, and cooks the picking in the north-central states. Each of the three deadly plants is stopped by at least two independent structural checks that are available in fruiting season. The entry also states plainly, three times, that habitat does not confer safety. I would let a beginner use this.

The Aesculus lookalike is rated 'deadly', consistent with all five other entries in foraging-species.ts that carry it (Acorns, Black walnut, Chestnut, Shagbark hickory nut) - checked programmatically, 5/5 rate it deadly. No consistency break.

THE DEADLY LOOKALIKE IS HANDLED AT OR ABOVE CORPUS BASELINE, AND SPECIFICALLY FOR THE SITUATION THE HARVEST ADVICE CREATES. The entry recognises that its own recommended method (gather what has fallen) destroys the leaf tell, and so supplies a tell that lives in the fruit itself: size/shape, smell, absence of seams, and a decisive cut-through. It explicitly refuses to let habitat do identification work ('Habitat does not identify a fallen fruit. Cutting it open does.') even though habitat overlap is real - Forest Service lists Ohio buckeye as a pawpaw stand associate and A. flava shares the same Appalachian coves.

IT DEMOLISHES THE INTUITIVE-BUT-WRONG TELL, WHICH IS THE HIGHEST-VALUE THING IN THE ENTRY. 'A green buckeye capsule dents under thumb pressure exactly as a softening fruit does. The thumb tells you whether a pawpaw is ripe and tells you nothing at all about what species you are holding.' This appears in parts, in the buckeye lookalike, and in harvest, and is repeated in the walnut lookalike with the Illinois Extension citation. This matches the identical squeeze-is-ripeness-never-identity warning already in the Black walnut entry, so the corpus is internally coherent on it.

NO REALISTIC PATH TO INGESTING BUCKEYE SURVIVES THE PROTOCOL. For a capsule to reach the mouth it must pass two independently impossible filters (be 2-6 in and oblong/kidney-shaped, when Aesculus is 1-2.25 in and globose/pear; and smell sweetly of banana and mango at arm's length, when Aesculus has no fruit smell before or after scratching), then survive 'cut the first fruit of the day and any fruit you did not personally see hanging on a pawpaw-leafed stem', then survive the mandatory halve-and-spoon prep in parts, which opens 100% of fruit before eating. 'If a single fruit does not cut like a pawpaw, cut the rest one at a time or tip the whole bag out' is the correct contamination response. 'Never taste to decide' is stated explicitly.

THE SIZE-OVERLAP HONESTY IS UNUSUAL AND CORRECT. It concedes the ranges nearly touch (a 2 in runt pawpaw vs a 2.25 in Ohio buckeye capsule) and downgrades size to 'a filter, not a verdict' rather than selling it as a rule. It then propagates that consistently: the persimmon lookalike notes 1-2 in persimmons are buckeye-capsule sized, and the A. parviflora lookalike notes 1-2.5 in small-flowered pawpaw fruit is too, each routing back to the cut. Internally consistent, no contradictions found across the five lookalikes.

TOXIC-PARTS PREPARATION IS COMPLETE AND MECHANISTICALLY CORRECT. Annonacin is correctly stated as heat-stable, so the entry correctly identifies the safety step as mechanical rather than thermal and pre-empts the specific error people make ('baking pawpaw bread does not detoxify pulp that has skin and crushed seed in it'). The no-blender / no-immersion-blender rule is the right concrete instruction because pulverising seed coat is the actual exposure route. Skin and seeds discarded, no swallowing or chewing seed, gloves for contact dermatitis per NC State. Potts arithmetic checks out: 0.07 mg/g x 50 g = 3.5 mg.

THE CHRONIC-NEUROTOXICITY RISK IS CALIBRATED, NOT OVERCLAIMED OR OMITTED. It reports the Guadeloupe atypical parkinsonism signal but correctly scopes it to heavy year-round consumption of a RELATED Annona rather than implying a bowl of September fruit is dangerous, and converts it into one actionable line ('don't make frozen pulp a daily year-round staple'). The idiosyncratic-reaction warning is properly operationalised as a tablespoon-then-wait-24-hours first-time test, and the GI complaints are correctly localised to black/split/insect-bored/fermented ground fruit.

NO MISSING DEADLY LOOKALIKE. I independently probed the plausible additions for a bottomland ground-gather in Aug-Oct: Osage orange (Maclura pomifera, 3-5 in green, drops Sept-Oct in midwest/southcentral bottomlands - not toxic, latex-bearing and visually unmistakable), mayapple (Podophyllum peltatum - same rich bottomland, soft yellow fruit, but herbaceous under an umbrella leaf and far smaller), hickory husks (four-valved, own entry) and pond apple (Annona glabra - edible). None is deadly, and every one is caught by the universal cut-open-and-check-for-custard-plus-rows-of-inch-long-flat-seeds rule. Aesculus is the only genuine deadly confusion and it is present.

TELLS ARE IN-SEASON AND REDUNDANT. The leaf tell (alternate simple obovate vs opposite palmately compound) is absolute and available throughout Aug-Oct when the trees are in leaf. The cut tell works on a bare fruit with no leaves. The smell tell is correctly restricted to ripe fruit and correctly labelled a filter. The zebra swallowtail indicator is sound (Asimina is its only larval host) and the deer-browse indicator is well documented. No tell depends on colour, which the entry repeatedly and correctly rejects as both a ripeness and an identity cue.

CONSERVATION AND LEGAL FRAMING IS APPROPRIATE AND ERRS SAFE. The ~0.45% natural fruit set, self-incompatible clonal biology and 'a fruiting patch is a genuinely uncommon event' framing justify the take-a-share instruction. The NY SGCN / NJ S2 claims are worth a maintainer spot-check, but they err toward 'admire and leave it', so a wrong call there carries no safety risk. The check-the-land-manager and NPS-units note is correct.

NIT, NON-BLOCKING: no Poison Control number. The Chestnut entry gives 1-800-222-1222 for the buckeye scenario; this entry does not. Low impact here because the protocol never puts an Aesculus seed in anyone's mouth (taste-testing is explicitly forbidden rather than described), but adding it would match corpus convention.

NIT, NON-BLOCKING: the 'three seams / splits into three valves' tell is hedged as 'as it dries', so it is weak on a freshly dropped green capsule. Correctly hedged rather than oversold, and size, smell and the cut are each independently sufficient without it, so the redundancy holds.

BEGINNER-SAFE VERDICT: yes. A beginner following this entry literally cannot get a buckeye into food, is told in plain terms which of their instincts (colour, squeeze, habitat) are worthless for identification, gets a five-second decisive test with an explicit cost ('costs you one fruit'), is given a preparation step that actually addresses the real toxin route, and is told to eat a tablespoon and wait before committing. Approve.

notes.name: Serviceberry (juneberry, saskatoon)
reasons: SCHEMA: clean. All twelve fields present and correctly typed. terrain values (edge, woodland, upland, wetland, disturbed) are all legal; caution 'expert' is legal and correct; every lookalikes[].danger is one of deadly/toxic/unpalatable with the correct 'danger' key (no illegal 'harmless'); regions is ['all']; months are plain ints. No serviceberry/Amelanchier entry already exists in foraging-species.ts (23 entries), so this is not a duplicate.

CAUTION IS CORRECT AND LOAD-BEARING: 'expert' is required here because Prunus (chokecherry/black cherry/cherry laurel) is graded deadly, and that grade is defensible — documented child fatalities from eating whole chokecherries seeds-and-all, and Carolina cherry laurel is lethal in every part. Note that this grade is what holds the entry at 'expert'; if a later editor downgrades Prunus and pokeweed to 'toxic', caution would have to drop to 'care'.

DEADLY-LOOKALIKE COVERAGE: I could not find a missing deadly confusion. The realistic dark-clustered-fruit hazards for a May-August pick are all present — Prunus, pokeweed, buckthorns (Rhamnus/Frangula incl. cascara and coffeeberry), the opposite-leaved ornamental group (privet/viburnum/dogwood/honeysuckle), cotoneaster, both nightshades, hawthorn. The operative rule (pome with a dried five-lobed calyx crown and 5-10 SOFT seeds, on an alternate-leaved, toothed, thornless woody plant) excludes every one of them, including ones not named.

CORPUS INCONSISTENCY (non-blocking, conservative direction): pokeweed is graded 'toxic' in all three existing entries that carry it (foraging-species.ts lines 194-195, 680-681, 1079-1080) and 'deadly' here. Same for Prunus — the sassafras entry grades black cherry 'toxic' (line ~1479). Both upgrades are arguably justified by the different exposure route (whole fruit with stones vs. a stray leaf), but the corpus should be reconciled in one direction rather than left split. Aesculus is not relevant to this entry and is not cited, so the deadly-everywhere rule is not violated.

TELL FLAW — the 'safety character' sentence in `parts` is factually wrong as written and should be fixed: 'every dangerous cluster-fruit this can be confused with is either a drupe with one hard stone (Prunus), a berry with three or four grooved stones (buckthorn), or a smooth-tipped berry with no crown at all (pokeweed, nightshade, privet)'. The entry's own cotoneaster lookalike says cotoneaster 'carries shiny black pomes that even keep a calyx remnant at the tip', and hawthorn is likewise a crowned pome. Not blocking, because the compound rule (crown AND soft seeds) still catches both — cotoneaster has 2-5 bony nutlets, hawthorn 1-5 — and both are disclosed with decisive checks lower down. But the enumeration should be rewritten to say the crown alone does not clear a fruit; the crown plus soft seeds does.

TELL RELIABILITY — the twig-snap smell test ('Prunus smells of bitter almond or marzipan, Amelanchier smells of nothing') can fail in the DANGEROUS direction: a large fraction of people cannot smell HCN/benzaldehyde at all, and would report 'nothing' from a chokecherry twig. It also sits oddly with this entry's own chemistry note that Amelanchier twigs are cyanogenic (prunasin). It is subordinate to the fruit dissection, which is correctly labelled decisive, and the entry separately warns never to use almond smell as positive confirmation — but the sentence should be qualified as one-way only (almond = walk away; no smell proves nothing).

MONTHS/REGIONS STRETCH: months [4,5,6,7] = May-August, 0-indexed, which is right for the genus overall — but combined with regions ['all'] it will surface serviceberry to an eastern user in August, when eastern Amelanchier is long finished and the eastern fencerow is instead filling with moonseed and Virginia creeper. The August window is a northern/high-elevation saskatoon phenomenon, and the entry says so only in passing inside the buckthorn tell; that qualifier belongs in habitat or harvest where a beginner will read it. Conversely, deep-South A. arborea can ripen in late April (month 3), which is excluded.

RANGE PROSE GAP: regions ['all'] is defensible (native Amelanchier in nearly every state plus universal ornamental planting), but the habitat prose covers East, Atlantic coastal plain, mountain West and Northwest and says nothing about southcentral. Compare the sassafras entry, which spells out its Oklahoma/Texas limits precisely. A southcentral reader gets no guidance that wild Amelanchier there is essentially confined to eastern OK/east TX and that what they will actually meet is a planted tree.

SUGGESTED ADDITIONS (not blocking, rule set already excludes them): moonseed (Menispermum canadense) — graded deadly twice elsewhere in this corpus, twines up through the same eastern edge shrubs, and is the exact 'hanging inside the plant you are picking' hazard mode the entry already invokes for bittersweet nightshade; Virginia creeper, same mode; and black chokeberry (Aronia), the closest crowned-pome match to serviceberry in eastern wet thickets, which is harmless but would read as an omission to anyone who has met it.

PREPARATION: correct and complete. Ripe Amelanchier fruit genuinely needs no treatment for safety, and the entry says so plainly rather than inventing a step. The 'THE REST OF THE PLANT IS NOT FOOD' block (prunasin in leaves/twigs/bark, worse when wilted, cited to CSU and the Majak 1980 cattle study) is appropriate, and the cross-warning that Prunus fruit must never go through a blender, juicer or food mill correctly anticipates the one dangerous interaction with this entry's own food-mill suggestion. One tightening worth making: say explicitly that the food mill is for a single-species basket, and that identification is per-plant before picking, not per-fruit after.

notes.name: Mulberry
reasons: NO MISSING DEADLY LOOKALIKE — checked adversarially and the list holds. Pokeweed, both nightshade groups (the two plants that actually stand under and grow up through a hedgerow mulberry), paper mulberry, Osage orange and the climbing Toxicodendron are all present. I specifically considered and rejected moonseed, Virginia creeper, buckthorn, privet and Amur honeysuckle: all produce single round berries that fail the compound-cylinder test, and all fruit in September or later, outside the Apr-Aug window. The corpus grades moonseed 'deadly' twice for the 'climbs up through the shrub you are picking' reason (elderberry and sassafras entries), but its September fruiting keeps it out of mulberry season, so its absence here is defensible.

SCHEMA IS CLEAN. caution/danger/terrain/regions values are all legal enum members ('harmless' is not used anywhere); months are 0-indexed integers in range; regions is ['all'], which is legal and correct since M. alba is naturalized in all six RegionIds and the range nuance (Texas mulberry in the Southwest, red mulberry in eastern bottomland) is correctly kept in habitat prose rather than in regions; terrain includes 'upland', which is justified by Texas mulberry on dry limestone canyon slopes. No existing 'Mulberry' entry in foraging-species.ts, so this is not a duplicate.

NO OMITTED SAFETY PREPARATION. Ripe mulberry genuinely is safe raw, and the entry is right to say so while stating flatly that cooking does NOT fix unripe fruit ('only waiting') — that is the correct and non-obvious call. Quantities and durations are given where they are needed (15-minute soak, 1 tbsp salt to 2 cups water), and the brine is explicitly labelled a quality step, not a safety one, which is honest.

SHARED-LOOKALIKE GRADING INCONSISTENCY (fix, not blocking): pokeweed is graded 'deadly' here but 'toxic' in all three other entries in the corpus that carry it — burdock root (line ~194), elderberry (line ~680) and Jerusalem artichoke (line ~1079) — and two of those are ROOT-exposure entries, where pokeweed is more dangerous than it is as a berry, not less. The entry's own evidence argues for 'toxic': NC State rates Phytolacca americana Poison Severity 'Medium' (I fetched the cited page), and its own Toxicon 2022 Kentucky citation records no deaths in 20 years. Resolve this corpus-wide. Note the knock-on: if pokeweed becomes 'toxic' here, then no lookalike in this entry is deadly and caution must drop to 'care' under the mechanical expert rule. I am not blocking because the error is in the conservative direction — the entry is over-rated, not under-rated.

MIS-CITED POKEBERRY DIMENSION in the most important lookalike. The tell says 'up to about 3/4 in wide' and the sources array attributes 'berries to ~3/4 in' to the NC State Phytolacca page — I fetched that page and it gives NO berry diameter at all. Real pokeberries run roughly 6-12 mm, and this corpus's own elderberry entry states '8-12 mm, flattened with a dimpled top and vertical ribs'. Correct the figure to ~1/4 to 1/2 in and drop the false attribution. Non-blocking because the pokeweed tell does not rest on it — herb-vs-woody-tree, the white latex test, and single-berry-vs-fused-cylinder are each independently decisive and all work every month.

WESTERN POISON OAK (Toxicodendron diversilobum) IS MISSING while regions is 'all'. The pre-touch instruction — 'look for the fuzzy rope, poison ivy's aerial rootlets make the bark look shaggy' — is an eastern T. radicans cue. In California, Oregon, Washington and parts of Arizona and Nevada the trunk-climbing urushiol plant is T. diversilobum, which climbs with far less conspicuous rootlets, and white mulberry is abundant in exactly the western irrigation-ditch, riparian and vacant-lot habitat this entry describes. The corpus already makes this substitution explicit in the elderberry entry ('in the West the contact hazard in elder thickets is poison oak instead'). Add it to the Toxicodendron lookalike. Non-blocking because the entry's primary rule — three fully separate leaflets on one shared stalk versus one lobed blade — catches western poison oak too.

INDICATOR OVERCLAIMS AND CONTRADICTS THE ENTRY'S OWN LOOKALIKE. 'Wildly different leaf shapes on the same twig clinch it... Almost nothing else in North America does that so freely, and every one of those leaves bleeds white latex' — paper mulberry does precisely that, with the same copious latex, and the entry's own Broussonetia lookalike says so ('same absurdly variable lobed and mitten-shaped leaves'). In southeastern and mid-Atlantic cities that combination lands on paper mulberry at least as often as on Morus. Rewrite 'clinch it' to carry the leaf-underside check (velvety grey-green versus smooth) forward into the indicator. Consequence is a wrong tree with an irritant latex and a severe pollen allergen, not a poisoning, so this is a fix rather than a block.

MONTHS/PROSE MISMATCH: months = [3,4,5,6,7] is April-August, but the harvest text says fruit is ripe 'from late March' in south Florida and the lower Rio Grande. Either add 2 or drop the late-March claim. The mismatch errs late — a south Florida user browsing March simply does not see the entry — so it costs fruit, not safety. The rest of the timing ladder (Gulf/central Texas late April-May, mid-South/mid-Atlantic late May-June, Midwest/Northeast June-July, interior West/PNW July into early August) matches month 7 correctly.

ARITHMETIC SLIP, cosmetic: 1 tbsp salt in 2 cups water is roughly 3.8% w/v, not 'about 5%'. Either restate as ~4% or raise the salt to about 1.5 tbsp per 2 cups. Nothing turns on it because the soak is correctly identified as a spotted-wing drosophila quality step, not a safety step.

PRESENTATION, cosmetic: 'parts' opens with 'Fully ripe fruit only' and then closes with a paragraph on Asian leaf tea and 1-deoxynojirimycin. The diabetes-medication warning is worth keeping, but it should say plainly that leaf harvest is outside the scope of this entry, so the paragraph cannot read as a leaf protocol. Note also a mild cross-entry tension: the sassafras entry (line ~1494) calls mulberry leaf edible silkworm fodder and grades it 'unpalatable', while this entry warns about leaf latex and DNJ. Both are true; a sentence in one of them would remove the apparent conflict.

WHAT MADE THIS APPROVABLE FOR A BEGINNER: the ripeness rule is specific and, crucially, states that COLOUR IS USELESS on M. alba and substitutes feel, which is the single most common way a beginner gets this wrong; the bucket-contamination path created by the tarp method is named and given a mandatory sorting step ('Never pour a tarp straight into a bucket and a bucket straight into a pan'); the published 'pokeweed is a fall berry' reassurance is explicitly retracted for the Gulf and mid-South; and every separation offered (latex, woody-versus-herbaceous, compound-versus-single, thorns on Maclura) works on the part actually harvested and in every month of the season. Osage orange 'unpalatable' and poison ivy 'toxic' both match the grades used in the black walnut and sassafras entries.
